results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across number sets (with >= 18 responses) of each set's overall yes-rate; observed above the null means sets differ in how generously they are generalized more than the model predicts (its set-level breadth is too compressed), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set differences.

results.name: drift_step_curvature
results.description: (yes-rate in trials 150-299 minus trials 0-149) minus (yes-rate in trials 300+ minus trials 150-299); observed above the null means the session drift toward "yes" is a front-loaded / saturating jump rather than the linear criterion relaxation the model assumes (below means the drift accelerates late).

results.name: last_step_direction_conflict
results.description: In 3+-example sets whose last step (second-last to last) points opposite to the overall first-to-last direction, yes-rate for outside-span targets within 30 beyond the span in the last-step direction minus those within 30 in the first-to-last direction; observed above the null means people's momentum follows the most recent step rather than the first-to-last travel the model uses (below means the first-to-last direction dominates even more than modelled).
results.code:
# name: last_step_direction_conflict
# description: In 3+-example sets whose last step (second-last to last) points opposite to the overall first-to-last direction, yes-rate for outside-span targets within 30 beyond the span in the last-step direction minus those within 30 in the first-to-last direction; observed above the null means people's momentum follows the most recent step rather than the first-to-last travel the model uses (below means the first-to-last direction dominates even more than modelled).
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ex = {s: [int(v) for v in s.split(",")] for s in sets}
    def ls(e):
        if len(e) < 3:
            return 0
        a = (e[-1] > e[0]) - (e[-1] < e[0]); b = (e[-1] > e[-2]) - (e[-1] < e[-2])
        return b if (a != 0 and b == -a) else 0
    lsd = ns.map({s: ls(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values.astype(int)
    hi = ns.map({s: max(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    lo = ns.map({s: min(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    above = (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 30)
    below = (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 30)
    with_last = ((lsd == 1) & above) | ((lsd == -1) & below)
    with_first = ((lsd == 1) & below) | ((lsd == -1) & above)
    if with_last.sum() == 0 or with_first.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[with_last].mean() - y[with_first].mean())

results.name: small_minus_large_magnitude_outside
results.description: Yes-rate for outside-span targets 1-15 beyond the span in sets whose examples are all <= 30, minus the same in sets whose examples are all >= 60; observed below the null means people generalize less (in absolute units) around small numbers than large ones — log/Weber-scaled magnitude similarity — which the model's linear size mismatch under-produces (above means the opposite).
results.code:
# name: small_minus_large_magnitude_outside
# description: Yes-rate for outside-span targets 1-15 beyond the span in sets whose examples are all <= 30, minus the same in sets whose examples are all >= 60; observed below the null means people generalize less (in absolute units) around small numbers than large ones — log/Weber-scaled magnitude similarity — which the model's linear size mismatch under-produces (above means the opposite).
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ex = {s: [int(v) for v in s.split(",")] for s in sets}
    hi = ns.map({s: max(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    lo = ns.map({s: min(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    d = np.maximum(np.maximum(lo - t, t - hi), 0)
    near = (d >= 1) & (d <= 15)
    small = near & (hi <= 30)
    large = near & (lo >= 60)
    if small.sum() == 0 or large.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[small].mean() - y[large].mean())

results.name: singleton_upward_minus_downward
results.description: In one-example sets, yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the example minus targets 1-20 below it; observed above the null means people generalize upward from a lone number more than the model (which has no direction of travel and so is symmetric for singletons) predicts (below means a downward bias).
results.code:
# name: singleton_upward_minus_downward
# description: In one-example sets, yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the example minus targets 1-20 below it; observed above the null means people generalize upward from a lone number more than the model (which has no direction of travel and so is symmetric for singletons) predicts (below means a downward bias).
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~ns.str.contains(",").values
    x = pd.to_numeric(ns.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    up = single & (t > x) & (t - x <= 20)
    dn = single & (t < x) & (x - t <= 20)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[up].mean() - y[dn].mean())

results.name: upward_bias_in_descending_sets
results.description: In 2+-example sets presented in descending order (last < first), yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the largest example minus targets 1-20 below the smallest; observed above the null means people keep a fixed upward (larger-number) generalization bias even when the sequence moves downward, which the model's purely order-directed momentum (predicting a downward advantage here) under-produces (below means momentum is stronger than modelled).
results.code:
# name: upward_bias_in_descending_sets
# description: In 2+-example sets presented in descending order (last < first), yes-rate for targets 1-20 above the largest example minus targets 1-20 below the smallest; observed above the null means people keep a fixed upward (larger-number) generalization bias even when the sequence moves downward, which the model's purely order-directed momentum (predicting a downward advantage here) under-produces (below means momentum is stronger than modelled).
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ex = {s: [int(v) for v in s.split(",")] for s in sets}
    desc = ns.map({s: len(e) >= 2 and e[-1] < e[0] for s, e in ex.items()}).values.astype(bool)
    hi = ns.map({s: max(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    lo = ns.map({s: min(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    up = desc & (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 20)
    dn = desc & (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 20)
    if up.sum() == 0 or dn.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[up].mean() - y[dn].mean())

results.name: next_term_extrapolation
results.description: In 2+-example sets with a nonzero last step, among outside-span targets 1-40 ahead of the span in the last step's direction, yes-rate for targets within 3 of the extrapolated next term (last + last step) minus the rest; observed above the null means people extrapolate the arithmetic step to predict the specific next number, which the model's smooth distance-based momentum cannot produce (below means no next-term peak, even less than modelled).
results.code:
# name: next_term_extrapolation
# description: In 2+-example sets with a nonzero last step, among outside-span targets 1-40 ahead of the span in the last step's direction, yes-rate for targets within 3 of the extrapolated next term (last + last step) minus the rest; observed above the null means people extrapolate the arithmetic step to predict the specific next number, which the model's smooth distance-based momentum cannot produce (below means no next-term peak, even less than modelled).
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ex = {s: [int(v) for v in s.split(",")] for s in sets}
    step = ns.map({s: (e[-1] - e[-2]) if len(e) >= 2 else 0 for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    la = ns.map({s: e[-1] for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    hi = ns.map({s: max(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    lo = ns.map({s: min(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ahead = ((step > 0) & (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 40)) | ((step < 0) & (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 40))
    nxt = la + step
    peak = ahead & (np.abs(t - nxt) <= 3)
    rest = ahead & ~peak
    if peak.sum() == 0 or rest.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[peak].mean() - y[rest].mean())

results.name: recency_inside_span
results.description: In 2+-example sets, among non-example targets strictly inside the span (min < t < max), yes-rate for those closer in size to the last-shown example than to the first minus the reverse; observed above the null means recency of the last example boosts generalization inside the span more than the model's memory-retention weighting produces (below means primacy / less recency than modelled).
results.code:
# name: recency_inside_span
# description: In 2+-example sets, among non-example targets strictly inside the span (min < t < max), yes-rate for those closer in size to the last-shown example than to the first minus the reverse; observed above the null means recency of the last example boosts generalization inside the span more than the model's memory-retention weighting produces (below means primacy / less recency than modelled).
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    ex = {s: [int(v) for v in s.split(",")] for s in sets}
    f = ns.map({s: e[0] for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    la = ns.map({s: e[-1] for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    hi = ns.map({s: max(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    lo = ns.map({s: min(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    kk = ns.map({s: len(e) for s, e in ex.items()}).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    exset = {s: set(e) for s, e in ex.items()}
    ident = np.fromiter((tt in exset[s] for tt, s in zip(t, ns.values)), bool, len(t))
    base = (kk >= 2) & ~ident & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    dl, dfst = np.abs(t - la), np.abs(t - f)
    cl, cf = base & (dl < dfst), base & (dfst < dl)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if cl.sum() == 0 or cf.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[cl].mean() - y[cf].mean())
